title: Checkpoint: Why Government?
objective: After this level you can explain what governments are for and how they are paid for.
summary: Aristotle called humans political animals. Chapter 1's answers to why government: shared rules, accepted authority, laws, public services paid for by taxes, and layers of government.

cards.headline: Why government at all? A Greek philosopher had an answer long before Hobbes.
cards.body: Aristotle said human beings are by nature political animals. We don't just happen to live in groups; living together is part of what we are. Anyone who could live entirely outside a community, he said, would be either a beast or a god.

cards.headline: First life, then the good life
cards.body: Aristotle wrote that the city-state comes into being for the sake of life, but exists for the sake of the good life. That's this chapter in one line. First, survival: Sumer's shared water, Hobbes's escape from a life that's nasty, brutish and short. Then, living well: schools, clean water and rules that let strangers play the same game.

items.label: Why rules?
points: So everyone plays the same game, from football to traffic
Laws bind a whole community and are enforced

items.label: Who decides?
points: Authority: power people accept as legitimate
The social contract asks why we obey

items.label: Who pays, and who does what?
points: National, regional and local layers share the work

cards.headline: Back at the helm
cards.body: Level 1 began with a ship. Now you can name its parts. The rules of the voyage are laws. Whoever holds the wheel needs authority, and the social contract asks why the crew goes along. The cargo everyone shares is public services. Taxes pay for the fuel. And the crew works on several decks at once, from the national government to the village council.

mascot.line: Ten levels in, and you can already steer a conversation about government.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: Humans are political animals, said Aristotle
Rules and laws let everyone play the same game
Taxes fund public services, shared across layers

questions.prompt: What did Aristotle call human beings?

options.label: Rational machines
options.rationale: Not his phrase; he stressed our need for community.

options.label: Naturally solitary
options.rationale: He said the opposite: only a beast or a god lives outside a community.

options.label: Free riders by nature
options.rationale: Free riding is Level 5's economics, not Aristotle.

questions.explanation: Aristotle said human beings are by nature political animals.

questions.prompt: What did Aristotle mean by saying the city-state exists "for the sake of the good life"?

options.label: Its purpose is living well, not just surviving
Its purpose is to make every citizen rich
options.rationale: Wealth isn't the point; living well is.

options.label: Only good people should be allowed to live in it
options.rationale: It's about the purpose of the community, not who may join.

options.label: It exists mainly in order to collect taxes
options.rationale: Taxes pay for things; they aren't the purpose.

questions.explanation: The city-state comes into being for the sake of life, but exists for the sake of the good life: living well, not just surviving.

questions.prompt: Why Government? checkpoint: which list puts these in order, oldest first?

options.label: Leviathan → Hammurabi's code → FA rules → Dagen H
options.rationale: Hammurabi's code (around 1750 BCE) is far older than Leviathan (1651).

options.label: Hammurabi's code → Leviathan → FA rules → Dagen H
Hammurabi's code → FA rules → Leviathan → Dagen H
options.rationale: Leviathan (1651) came before the FA's rules (1863).

options.label: FA rules → Hammurabi's code → Dagen H → Leviathan
options.rationale: Hammurabi's code is the oldest by thousands of years.

questions.explanation: Hammurabi's code (around 1750 BCE), Leviathan (1651), the FA's rules (1863), Dagen H (1967).

questions.prompt: Back to Level 3: a monarch who inherits the throne holds which kind of authority, in Weber's scheme?

options.label: Charismatic
options.rationale: Charismatic authority rests on personal qualities, not inheritance.

options.label: Legal-rational
options.rationale: Legal-rational authority rests on laws and offices.

options.label: None: inheritance gives only power
options.rationale: An inherited throne is Weber's example of traditional authority.

questions.explanation: Traditional authority rests on long-standing custom, like inheriting a throne.

questions.prompt: Canada's municipal governments and India's village panchayats are both examples of what?

options.label: National government
options.rationale: Both are the layer closest to home, not the national one.

options.label: International organizations
options.rationale: Both work inside a single country.

options.label: Nation-states
options.rationale: A nation-state is a whole country, not a local council.

questions.explanation: Both are the local layer of government: the one closest to your front door.
